paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: For most of the past two centuries, economic growth has been treated as an unquestioned good. It is associated with rising incomes, longer lives and declining poverty, and political leaders are judged by how fast their economies expand. Yet a growing number of economists and environmentalists ask whether endless growth is compatible with a finite planet. I will argue that the question is legitimate, but that the answer is more complicated than either side suggests.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The environmental case against growth rests on the observation that, historically, economic output and resource use have risen together. More production has meant more energy, more raw materials and more waste. Global carbon emissions, despite improvements in efficiency, have continued to rise in line with the economy for most of the industrial era. If this link cannot be broken, growth must eventually collide with the limits of the biosphere.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Defenders of growth reply that the link can be broken, a process called decoupling. Some wealthy countries, including Britain and Sweden, have in recent decades reduced territorial emissions while their economies expanded. The difficulty is that much of this reduction reflects the relocation of manufacturing abroad, so the emissions are counted in other countries, and that the pace of decoupling is nowhere near fast enough to meet climate targets. Absolute decoupling on the scale required has not yet been demonstrated at a global level.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: An alternative proposal, degrowth, argues that rich countries should deliberately reduce production and consumption in some sectors, while sharing work and improving public services. Its advocates point to evidence that beyond a certain income, additional wealth adds little to happiness. But the proposal faces a political problem: modern economies depend on growth to maintain employment, finance pensions and service debt, and voters are rarely enthusiastic about contraction. A managed shrinkage would require institutions that do not yet exist.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: My own view is that the framing as growth versus no growth is unhelpful. What matters is what grows and what shrinks. An economy in which clean energy, education and healthcare expand while fossil fuel extraction declines could grow in monetary terms and still reduce its environmental impact. Whether such a transition can happen quickly enough is uncertain, and prudence suggests planning for both possibilities: preparing for a world of continued growth, and for one in which growth stalls.
